title: The Last Run
subtitle: Friday 15 to Monday 18 July 1881: The Canvass, One More Run for No Pay, a Station That Won't Sell You a Horse, the Puerco in Flood and Ten O'Clock in Old Town

setting.name: Santa Teresita, the Albuquerque road and Albuquerque's Old Town, 15 to 18 July
setting.description: Everything the party has won has to go seventy miles. The federal grand jury is sworn at the courthouse in Albuquerque's Old Town at ten o'clock on Monday 18 July. The Company's suit to quiet its title to the commons is on the docket that morning and goes by default if the grant doesn't answer. Any contest of the election has to be filed the same day. The witnesses are in Santa Teresita: Tiburcio, Jethro Petree, Hob Linnet or Fenton Rusk if they are held, Rufina, Victoriano Romero's statement. So are the evidence and the act of possession. The mail now goes through the Company's town. So does the telegraph, and so does the train. Cyprian Ludlow offers his coach. One more run, he says, no contract and no pay, and this one is his. The Company has three days and every man it can hire to stop it.
setting.atmosphere: The road at the height of the rains. Mornings are clear and washed, with the mesas sharp as cut paper and the llano gone suddenly green. Afternoons are thunder, hail, sheets of rain marching across the country, and arroyos running brown and roaring. The coach is heavy with people and paper and fear. Its old leather creaks, its six horses are the last good ones Ludlow owns, and Jethro or Rafael sings to them because that is how it has always been done. The stations are a string of beads: La Mesita, still the line's, with coffee and gossip; the Puerco, the Company's now, with locked corrals; the Ceja, with the whole Rio Grande valley below it at dawn. Then the cottonwoods of Atrisco, the bridge, and Old Town's plaza on a Monday morning, with the church of San Felipe de Neri, the courthouse, the lawyers and the bells.

keyLocations.name: Santa Teresita and the canvass
keyLocations.description: Friday 15 July. In the courthouse's long room the county commissioners canvass the precinct returns and certify the result, with the Company's lawyer from Albuquerque, Thurman Ames, objecting to everything. Ludlow's corrals, where la Doña is being greased and her last six horses shod by Royal Penhallow or the plaza smith. Ludlow's offer is made on Doña Eufemia's portal on Friday evening.
features: The canvass table, the five returns, the poll books with their challenges written in, and Thurman Ames's long list of objections
La Doña in the corral: the coach that was robbed, with a .50 hole through the seat back and a bullet scar on the lamp
The comisión's chest from the church, carried to the station on Friday night with the act of possession and the grant's answer inside
The jail, where Hob Linnet or Rusk is held, if they are, with two deputies and a lamp burning all night
encounters: No set combat at the canvass. Thurman Ames and two Company clerks, and a room that wants to throw them out of the window
On Friday night, an attempt to burn the coach in the corral: two men with coal oil (Hired Gun) sent from Paragon, unless someone is watching
secrets: The canvass. If The Vote went the plaza's way, the commissioners certify Santa Teresita and Celestino Trujillo. Ames announces that the Company will contest the result in the district court on Monday, on the ground that 'a band of armed strangers intimidated the Paragon poll'. If the Company won, the People's party must file its own contest by Monday with the poll books and the envelopes. Either way, the case goes to Albuquerque, and so must the evidence.

Thurman Ames has a second paper in his case, which he shows nobody. The Company bought Cyprian Ludlow's $4,000 note from the Bank of the Rio Abajo on Thursday, and it has a writ of attachment from an Albuquerque justice to seize the line's coach and horses for the debt. A deputy constable will serve it at the Albuquerque end of the bridge on Monday morning (see the bridge). Insight DC 15 to see that Ames is too pleased with himself, or Investigation DC 14 to see the writ in his case.

Jethro Petree asks to drive. He says it to Ludlow in front of everyone on the portal: 'Let me take her in. Let me take her in, Cyprian, and then hang me.' Ludlow looks at him for a long time and says it's not his to decide. It's whoever is riding. If the party agrees, Jethro drives like a man possessed and will die before he lets the coach stop. If they don't, Rafael drives, and Jethro rides inside as a witness and weeps.
The Company knows the coach is going. Uriah Quist read Montaño's wire to the plaza on Thursday. Whatever else happens, the Company's men will be on the road.

keyLocations.name: The Puerto de Piedra and La Mesita
keyLocations.description: The first twenty miles. The coach goes through the Puerto de Piedra again, at dawn on Saturday, past the juniper where the red rag was. La Mesita station, twenty miles out, is still Ludlow's: an adobe on a little flat-topped hill with a corral, a well, a keeper named Bonifacio Ulibarri, his wife, nine children and the line's last fresh team.
features: The gap at dawn: the black boulders, the bend, the place on the box where Lon sat
La Mesita's corral and its six fresh horses, the last the line owns east of the plaza
The keeper's wife, who has heard from a sheepherder that riders crossed the road going east at midnight
A view east from the mesa across twenty miles of llano to the line of the Rio Puerco's cottonwoods
encounters: At the Puerto de Piedra, a felled tree and two riflemen (Bandit Sharpshooter) on the north outcrop again, with orders to shoot the lead horses and stop the coach. They don't expect it to come through the gap at a gallop
No combat at La Mesita, unless the party is careless with the horses
secrets: The Company's plan is to stop the coach, not to massacre it. A massacre on the road would bring the federal government. The riflemen at the gap are to kill the lead horses, the men at the Puerco are to deny the teams, and the riders at the Ceja are to take the comisión's chest and the witnesses. Killing is for Rendell, if he lives, and he means to do it himself.

Bonifacio Ulibarri at La Mesita has been offered $200 for the station and his horses by the Company, payable when the coach fails to arrive. He has refused, and he'll tell the party so with some pride. His eldest son, Facundo, sixteen, rides like Tiburcio and wants to come.

From La Mesita's mesa, anyone with field glasses (Perception DC 13) sees, far off to the east along the Puerco, smoke where no one should be camping: the Company's men are at the Puerco station already.

If Victoriano Romero trusts the party, there's a message at La Mesita in Spanish, left by a Laguna rider: the Company's men are at the Puerco station, and a Laguna family's horse herd is grazing the Puerco bottoms a mile upstream of the crossing, and will trade with Señor Ludlow for silver. 'At a fair price,' it says. 'We are not giving anything away.'

keyLocations.name: The Puerco station and the crossing
keyLocations.description: Forty miles out, at the Rio Puerco: the adobe station, the ramada and the well where the coach slept on the first night of the campaign, and the quarter-mile of sand riverbed beside it. From 8 July the station is the Company's. Doroteo Griego, the old keeper, is still there, now on the Company's payroll, with six Company men, locked corrals and orders to sell nothing to the Rio Seco line. The Puerco in July is dry at noon and a torrent at four.
features: The station's locked corral with the line's own twelve horses inside it, now Company property
Doroteo Griego, ashamed, with the keys on a ring at his belt
The riverbed, a quarter-mile of firm sand with a trickle down the middle, and the far bank thirty feet high with a single ramp for wagons
The thunderheads over the mountains to the west, building every afternoon from about one o'clock
encounters: Six Company men at the station (two Agency Detectives and four Hired Guns), who are there to deny the horses, not to fight a war, and will fight if the party takes them
The flood: a flash flood down the Rio Puerco at about four on Sunday afternoon, a brown wall of water six feet high, running 1d4 hours
secrets: Doroteo Griego has the keys and a conscience. He drove for Ludlow before he kept the station, and he was at the Puerco station when Lon Brisbane laughed at Jethro. Persuasion DC 14 (advantage if Ludlow or Jethro asks him) and he lets the line's horses out the back of the corral at dusk and says they broke out. It costs him his job and maybe more, and he does it anyway if he is asked like a friend. Intimidation works too, and he will hate whoever used it.

The Laguna family's horse herd a mile upstream, if Victoriano arranged it: twenty horses, two Laguna herders, an older man and his nephew, who will trade six for Ludlow's six blown ones and $60 in silver, which is a fair price and no more. They expect courtesy and give it. They will not fight the Company's men. That is not their quarrel, and they say so.

The flood. At about four on Sunday the sky over the Puerco's upper basin goes black, and a man with Weather Eye, a Scout's sense or Survival DC 14 hears it coming ten minutes before it arrives. A coach in the riverbed when it comes is swept away. A coach on the near bank is held up for 1d4 hours while the Company's riders close in. A coach that crosses before it, at the gallop, with the water coming, is a scene the players will remember.

If the coach is held on the near bank by the flood, the Company's riders from the station come for it in the rain. The party has the coach, the bank, the storm and whatever it took from the station. The riders want the chest and the witnesses. The river is the clock.

keyLocations.name: The Ceja and Atrisco
keyLocations.description: Fifty-eight miles out the road climbs the Ceja, the long escarpment on the west side of the Rio Grande valley, and from the top at dawn on Monday you can see Albuquerque: the cottonwoods along the river, Old Town's church towers and New Town's smoke a mile and a half beyond. Then six miles down the grade and through Atrisco's fields and orchards to the river. The Ceja station is kept by Casilda Gutiérrez, the widow of Ludlow's old keeper, who has kept it alone for three years for no pay since the contract was cut.
features: The top of the Ceja at dawn, with the whole valley below and the road dropping away in long loops
Casilda Gutiérrez's station: two rooms, a corral, a well, and four old horses that she has kept fit for the line out of stubbornness
The grade down, steep, rutted, with a drop on one side and arroyos cutting across it
Atrisco: a farming village of adobe, acequias and orchards, the last place before the river
encounters: On the Ceja grade at dawn: the Company's last throw. Cade Rendell (Fast Gun) if he lives, or Shad Sorrel (Bandit Sharpshooter) if he doesn't, with six riders (Hired Gun or Road Agent), coming up behind the coach on fresh horses for a running fight down the grade (combat.json chases)
No combat in Atrisco. The vecinos come out to watch the coach go by, and some of them follow it to the river
secrets: Casilda Gutiérrez has four horses that are old and sound, and coffee. She also has her late husband's shotgun, and she will ride down the grade on the box if anyone is hurt. She has been waiting three years for the line to need her again.

Rendell, if he lives, has given up on the Company. Rusk is ruined and Coldiron won't pay him. He's here for the same reason he called the showdown in Paragon: to be the man who stopped the last coach. If he can't stop it on the grade, he'll ride ahead to the Old Town plaza and wait in front of the courthouse, because a man who kills a witness on the courthouse steps will be remembered.

The grade is a chase, three to five rounds, Animal Handling on the box against the riders' Riding. Complications from combat.json chases: an arroyo across the road, a freight wagon coming up, a goat herd, a washout, a burro train of firewood. If the riders catch the coach, they try to board it for the chest. If the coach loses a wheel, it is three miles to the river on foot with the chest and the witnesses.

Atrisco's people know Ludlow and know la Doña, and have heard what the coach is carrying from a Laguna section hand who came through on Sunday. A party that stops to ask for help gets a dozen armed farmers on mules to escort them to the bridge. The Company's riders won't follow them into a village.

keyLocations.name: Albuquerque: the bridge, Old Town plaza and the courthouse
keyLocations.description: Monday 18 July. The bridge over the Rio Grande, the road through the fields to Old Town, and the old plaza: low adobe buildings with portals on four sides, the church of San Felipe de Neri on the north side, and the county courthouse where the district court sits for its July term from ten o'clock. Judge Ives Maitland presides. Licenciado Ezequiel Montaño is waiting on the courthouse steps with his watch in his hand. The federal grand jury is being sworn. The Company's lawyer, Thurman Ames, and Everard Coldiron came by train on Sunday. New Town, the depot, the Bank of the Rio Abajo and the Southwestern Express office are a mile and a half east.
features: The bridge, with a toll-keeper's shed at the Albuquerque end and a deputy constable waiting there with a paper
Old Town plaza: a cottonwood, a bandstand, the church's two towers, vendors, carts, lawyers, loafers
The courthouse steps, where Montaño waits
The clock in the church tower, which runs four minutes fast, as everyone in Albuquerque knows except the people who are racing it
encounters: At the bridge, a deputy constable with a writ of attachment for the coach and horses (Deputy), and two Company men to help him (Agency Detective)
On the plaza, Cade Rendell (Fast Gun), if he lives and wasn't stopped on the Ceja, waiting in front of the courthouse to kill a witness in front of the town
secrets: The writ of attachment is lawful. The Company bought Ludlow's $4,000 note and is seizing the line's coach and horses for it. It does not attach the passengers, the witnesses or the chest, and a Back East character or Montaño can say so (Investigation DC 12). Then everyone walks the last mile. Or someone pays: the Southwestern Express Company's reward for the box, which Milo Thackery will advance against a deputy marshal's word, or Darius Crandall, the bank's cashier, whose numbered notes were used to buy votes. He is honest and furious, and he will go to the bridge and tell the deputy that the bank's sale of the note to the Company is suspended pending inquiry (Persuasion DC 13 with him on Saturday by wire from La Mesita, or in person if anyone rides ahead).

Judge Ives Maitland is a careful, slow, honest New Englander who has been on the territorial bench for six years and has heard every grant case and every election contest the district has. He'll take the grand jury's evidence, Montaño's answer and the contests in order, in public. He wants originals and witnesses, not stories. The act of possession, the schedule beside the notes, the envelope bill and Coldiron's letter are what he wants.

If Rusk reached Albuquerque on the 6:40 train, he's at the courthouse with Ames, ready to swear that the party and the plaza stole the election. Once Tiburcio, Jethro and Linnet are on the stand, and Venancio's letter in Rusk's own hand is read, his story falls apart, and he will try to save himself by giving the court Coldiron. Coldiron, on the courthouse bench in a white suit, discovers that he's in the copybook.

Rendell on the plaza. If he's alive, he's waiting by the bandstand, alone, with the sun behind the church at his back, for whoever comes first up the courthouse steps with the chest. It is the campaign's last showdown, in front of a city, and the same choice as Paragon: draw, arrest, or something cleverer. Federal marshals are inside the courthouse, and a Deputy U.S. Marshal who calls them out has a posse in thirty seconds. Rendell knows it, and it's why he chose the steps.

synopsis: The last run of the Rio Seco line, with no contract, no pay and everything on board. On Friday the canvass certifies the election, or the plaza loses it, and either way the Company's lawyer announces a contest in the district court on Monday. That night someone tries to burn the coach in its corral. Cyprian Ludlow makes his offer on the portal: la Doña, his last six horses and the road, one more time. Jethro Petree asks to drive her. The party decides who rides: the witnesses, the evidence, the comisión's chest with the act of possession and the grant's answer, Laguna's protest, and the prisoners if they have any. They decide who drives. The coach leaves before dawn on Saturday. At the Puerto de Piedra there are riflemen again, ordered to kill the lead horses. At La Mesita there are fresh horses and a warning. At the Puerco station, which the Company owns now, the corrals are locked and six Company men are waiting, and the line's own horses are inside. A Laguna family's herd a mile upstream will trade at a fair price, if the party has earned the arrangement. On Sunday afternoon the Rio Puerco comes down in flood. The coach can cross ahead of it or wait while the Company's riders close in. On Monday at dawn, on the grade down the Ceja, Cade Rendell or Shad Sorrel comes for the chest in a running fight. At the bridge a deputy has a writ to seize the coach for Ludlow's debts. In Old Town, at ten o'clock, Licenciado Montaño waits on the courthouse steps with his watch, and Rendell may be waiting at the bandstand. The court sits. Who reaches it, and with what, decides the robbery, the election, the commons and the line.
hook: Friday 15 July, evening, on Doña Eufemia's portal, after the canvass. Cyprian Ludlow stands with his hat in his hands, and for the first time in the campaign he looks every one of his sixty-six years. 'The mail's not mine to carry any more,' he says. 'The contract's gone, and the Company holds my note, and I expect it'll take the horses inside the month. But la Doña is greased and the last six are shod, and the road to Albuquerque is still a public road. I'd like to make one more run. No contract, no fare, no pay. This one's mine.' He looks round at all of you. 'I'd be honoured to have you aboard. With whatever you're carrying.' Behind him, in the dark of the corral, an old man climbs up onto the coach's box and sits there with the lines in his hands.

conclusions.conclusion: The robbery reaches the grand jury
clues: A4 and A5: the .50 ball and Rendell's rifle; Tiburcio's eyewitness account
B6 and C6: Jethro Petree's or Hob Linnet's confession, and Rusk's if he talks
C1 and C2: the bank's schedule beside the notes from the envelopes
C3 and C5: Cazenove's bill and Coldiron's copybook letter

conclusions.conclusion: The grant answers the Company's suit
clues: E5: the act of possession of 1768, 'in common for all'
E3: the Company's petition, to remove 'all occupants' from the whole grant
E4 and Laguna's protest: the moved corner at the Cerro Colorado
Don Policarpio's, Rufina's and Don Fermín's testimony of a hundred years' common use

conclusions.conclusion: The election stands, or is overturned, on evidence
clues: D2: the Paragon poll list and the challenges in the poll book
D4 and D5: the repeaters and the yellow tickets
Venancio Chávez's letter from Rusk, offering to forgive his note for a false count
The miners' testimony, and the envelopes

acts.title: Friday and Saturday: Load the Coach
acts.description: The decision and the departure. The canvass sets the legal stakes; Ludlow's offer sets the road. Let the players choose who rides, who drives, what they carry and what they leave behind. Every choice costs something: a witness left at the plaza can't testify, and one taken on the coach is a target. Then the road begins with the place where the campaign began.
objectives: See the canvass through, and know what the Company will claim in court
Keep the coach from burning on Friday night
Choose the passengers, the cargo and the driver
Get through the Puerto de Piedra and reach La Mesita with the coach and team intact

scenes.name: The Canvass
scenes.description: Friday morning at the courthouse's long room. The three county commissioners, two People's and one Progress, open the five returns and the poll books and add them up in public. Thurman Ames, the Company's lawyer from Albuquerque, objects to the Plata Vieja return, the challenges at Paragon, the red crosses on the tickets (which he calls 'marked ballots') and the presence of armed strangers. The result is whatever The Vote produced. Whichever side lost will contest it in the district court on Monday, so the evidence has to go to Albuquerque. Ames also carries the writ for Ludlow's coach, and doesn't mention it.
scenes.readAloud: The long room is hot and packed, and it smells of whitewash and old grain and too many people. At the pine table under the crucifix sit three men with pens: a sheep rancher, a storekeeper and a Paragon lumber dealer, with five canvas bags in front of them sealed with wax. One by one the seals are broken, the poll books opened, the tally sheets read out and added on a slate. At the end of the table a tall thin man in a black frock coat, with a lawyer's stoop and a lawyer's voice, stands up at every third line to say, 'The Company objects,' and sits down again. He has a leather case on his knees, and every so often, when he thinks nobody's looking, he pats it, the way a man pats a pocket with money in it.

skillChecks.success: Ames is too pleased with himself for a man who is losing, or too calm for one who's winning. There's something in his case he's saving. Watch him at noon, and you see him give a folded paper to a man who rides off east on a fast horse.
skillChecks.failure: A lawyer objecting. That's what lawyers are for.

skillChecks.success: In Ames's case, while he's at dinner at Doña Eufemia's table: a copy of an assignment of Cyprian Ludlow's $4,000 note from the Bank of the Rio Abajo to the Company, dated Thursday, and a writ of attachment against the line's coach and horses, to be served 'at the Albuquerque end of the Rio Grande bridge'. Forewarned is everything. You can wire the bank's cashier from La Mesita's nearest telegraph, or ride ahead, or plan to walk the last mile.
skillChecks.failure: Ames keeps the case on his knees through dinner, and through dessert.

skillChecks.success: If the plaza won, you help the commissioners certify it cleanly, with every challenge and objection written into the record, so that Monday's contest is fought on the plaza's ground. If the plaza lost, you help Celestino and Montaño's clerk draw up the contest papers properly. Either way, the papers that go into the chest are in order.
skillChecks.failure: The canvass ends in a shouting match, and the record is a mess that Ames will make the most of on Monday.

scenes.name: Ludlow's Offer
scenes.description: Friday evening on the portal. Ludlow's offer, Jethro's request, and the party's choice of who rides. The obvious cargo: the comisión's chest (the act of possession, the grant's answer, Laguna's protest), the evidence box (the schedule, notes, envelopes, the Cazenove bill, the copybook page, the plat, Venancio's letter), and the witnesses (Tiburcio, Jethro, Rufina, Don Policarpio if he can stand the road, which he insists he can, and Hob Linnet or Rusk in irons if held). That is too many people for nine seats and too much for one coach. At about midnight two men with coal oil come over the corral wall to burn la Doña, unless someone is sitting up with her.
scenes.readAloud: The portal is lit with lanterns, and half the plaza is there: Doña Eufemia in black silk with her arms folded, Celestino with a satchel of papers, Don Policarpio in a chair with a blanket over his knees, Rufina, Tiburcio, Doña Luz holding her husband's coat. Out in the corral la Doña stands with her pole up on its prop and her doors open, greased and polished. You can still see the hole the big ball made through her seat back. Jethro Petree is sitting on her box in the dark. When Ludlow finishes speaking, the old driver climbs down and comes across the yard into the lantern light and stands in front of his employer of thirteen years with his hat crushed in his hands. 'Let me take her in,' he says. 'Let me take her in, Cyprian, and then let them hang me. I'd not ask it if I could think of a single other thing to ask.'

skillChecks.success: Jethro means it. If he drives, he will drive as no man in the territory can, and he'll die before he lets the coach stop. Rafael Candelaria, beside him, wants to drive too, and wants Jethro to be allowed to, and can't say either. Whatever you decide, decide it out loud, in front of them both.
skillChecks.failure: An old man, a young one and a coach. You can't tell what either of them would do on the box under fire.

skillChecks.success: You settle the passengers and the cargo without anyone feeling left behind. Don Policarpio is persuaded to send his sworn statement and his great-grandson instead of himself, Rufina rides with the chest, Venancio takes a horse alongside, and the prisoners ride on the roof in irons under guard. The coach is heavy but balanced, and the people who stay behind know why.
skillChecks.failure: Don Policarpio insists on coming. He's seventy-eight and frail, and the road will be very hard on him (CON save each day or a level of exhaustion; Zadok or Doña Paz can help). He'll be magnificent in court, if he gets there.

skillChecks.success: At about midnight two men come over the corral wall with a can of coal oil, and you're awake to see them. They're Paragon men, paid $20 each, and they're more frightened than dangerous. Taken alive, they say the order came from Ames's rider and the money from Coldiron's clerk.
skillChecks.failure: The first you know is the smell of coal oil and a flare of light at la Doña's rear boot. It takes everyone on the plaza with buckets to save her. She runs on Saturday with a scorched boot and a smell of smoke, and the party has lost two hours of sleep.

scenes.name: The Puerto de Piedra, Again
scenes.description: Saturday, an hour after dawn, nine miles out: the same gap and the same bend. A felled juniper across the road beyond the bend, and two riflemen on the north outcrop with orders to kill the lead horses. This time the party knows the ground. A driver who knows what's coming takes the grade at a walk, then whips up at the bend and goes round the tree on the south verge at a gallop, which the riflemen don't expect. Or the party sends riders up onto the outcrop ahead of the coach, or goes round by the arroyo. It should feel like the campaign coming full circle.
scenes.readAloud: The light comes up gold over the llano behind you as the coach climbs into the gap, and there is the bend, and the outcrop, and the juniper on the ridge where the red rag hung. It isn't there. Nobody on the coach says anything. On the box, whoever is driving gathers the lines a little shorter and speaks to the leaders, and the horses' ears go back and forward. Then, from the rocks to the north, very faintly, comes the double click of a rifle hammer being drawn back, and the driver says, quite softly, 'Hold on to something,' and stands up and lets the whip go out over the leaders' heads with a crack like a pistol.

skillChecks.success: The coach comes round the bend at a full gallop, finds the felled tree, and goes round it on the south verge with two wheels in the air and the passengers on the floor. The riflemen get one shot each and miss the leaders. You're through. (Jethro driving gives advantage; so does a Cowhand's Saddle-Born on a horse alongside, steadying the leaders.)
skillChecks.failure: A lead horse is hit and goes down. The coach slews and stops beside the tree, and the riflemen have it under their guns. Someone has to deal with them, and someone has to cut the dead horse out of the traces, under fire.

skillChecks.success: Two riders sent ahead up the outcrop before the coach comes find the riflemen from behind. They're the Company's men, not Rendell's, and they surrender quickly. Taken alive, they say they were told to shoot horses, not people, and that 'the Texan' would do the rest at the Ceja.
skillChecks.failure: The riflemen hear you coming and open fire on the riders instead of the horses. That's better for the coach and worse for the riders.

skillChecks.success: If Jethro is driving, he takes the bend with his face like stone, and on the far side, when the gap is behind and the horses have slowed to a trot, he takes off his hat and holds it over his heart for a moment, passing the place where Lon died. Anyone who sees it understands that whatever else happens, he has paid something here.
skillChecks.failure: The driver doesn't look back.

encounters: Friday midnight at the corral: two Paragon men with coal oil (Hired Gun, but frightened; they surrender if challenged)
Saturday dawn at the Puerto de Piedra: two Company riflemen (Bandit Sharpshooter) on the north outcrop, three-quarters cover, ordered to shoot the lead horses and the coach's team rather than people

acts.title: Saturday Night and Sunday: The Puerco
acts.description: The middle of the road and the hardest part. La Mesita has fresh horses and a warning. The Puerco station, the Company's, has locked corrals and six men. The Laguna herd upstream may trade. Then the river. The flood comes at about four on Sunday whether the party is ready or not. Run it as a clock, and tell the players they can hear the thunder.
objectives: Change teams at La Mesita, and learn what is waiting at the Puerco
Get fresh horses at the Puerco: from the Company's corral, from Doroteo, or from the Laguna herd
Cross the Rio Puerco before the flood, or hold the near bank until it falls
Keep the chest and the witnesses out of the Company's hands

scenes.name: La Mesita
scenes.description: Saturday about noon at Ludlow's La Mesita station, twenty miles out. Bonifacio Ulibarri, his wife, nine children and the line's last fresh team. Bonifacio refused the Company's $200 and is proud of it. His wife heard from a sheepherder that riders crossed the road going east at midnight. From the top of the little mesa, field glasses show smoke at the Puerco station. If Victoriano arranged it, a Laguna rider has left a message about the herd upstream. Bonifacio's son Facundo, sixteen, wants to ride with the coach and is very good on a horse.
scenes.readAloud: La Mesita is a little flat-topped hill with an adobe on it, a corral, a well, a crowd of children, and a woman standing in the doorway with her apron full of eggs. A short broad man in a straw hat is already opening the corral gate before the coach has stopped. 'Don Cyprian! They told me the line was finished. I said, Don Cyprian is not finished. Six fresh, all shod, all fed. The Company offered me two hundred dollars for them on Tuesday. I told the man he could kiss my mule.' He grins, and stops grinning. 'My wife says riders went by last night, going east. Eight, ten. They did not stop for water. Men who do not stop for water at La Mesita are not going to a dance.'

skillChecks.success: From the top of the mesa with field glasses: smoke at the Puerco station, twenty miles east, where the keeper never cooks at midday, and the glint of a rifle barrel on the station roof. The Company is there already. If there is a Laguna message, it says where the herd is.
skillChecks.failure: Twenty miles of shimmering llano. You can't see anything out there but heat.

skillChecks.success: You get the fresh team into the traces in ten minutes, and the tired one into the corral for Bonifacio to rest. You also see which of the new six is the steady leader and which will bolt at gunfire, and swap them, which will matter later.
skillChecks.failure: The change takes forty minutes, and one of the new leaders is skittish. You'll have disadvantage on the first Animal Handling check under fire.

skillChecks.success: If anyone rides north from here to the River Line's telegraph at its Puerco bridge, twelve miles off, where the operator is a railroad man and not the Company's, a wire reaches Darius Crandall at the bank in Albuquerque by evening: the Company holds Ludlow's note and means to seize the coach. Crandall wires back on Sunday that the sale of the note is 'suspended pending the bank's inquiry'. The writ at the bridge is now worthless.
skillChecks.failure: There's no wire you can trust within thirty miles. The bridge will have to be dealt with at the bridge.

scenes.name: The Company's Station
scenes.description: Saturday evening at the Puerco station, forty miles out. The line's twelve horses are in the station's locked corral, and they are the Company's now. Six Company men, two Albuquerque detectives and four hired guns, have orders to sell nothing and give nothing. Doroteo Griego, the old keeper, has the keys and a conscience. The party's options: take the horses by force, which is a gunfight and, strictly, theft; persuade Doroteo, who lets them out the back at dusk; trade with the Laguna herd a mile upstream, if Victoriano arranged it; or go on with a blown team at half speed. The Laguna herders expect a fair trade and courtesy, and will not be drawn into the Company's quarrel.
scenes.readAloud: The station is as you left it three weeks ago: the low adobe square, the ramada, the well sweep, the wide pale sand of the riverbed. But the ramada is empty and there is no fiddle, and a man with a rifle on the roof stands up as the coach comes in sight and calls something down into the yard. Five more men come out and stand in front of the corral gate with their thumbs in their belts. Inside the corral, behind them, a dozen horses you know lift their heads and whicker at the coach team. Ludlow's horses. In the station doorway an old man in a leather apron with a ring of keys at his belt looks at the coach, at Ludlow on the step, and at the ground.

skillChecks.success: Doroteo Griego can't meet Ludlow's eye. Asked as a friend, by Ludlow or Jethro or anyone he trusts, he says nothing at all. But at dusk, while the Company men are at supper, the back rails of the corral are down and the line's horses are in the riverbed, and Doroteo says in the morning that they broke out in the night. He loses his job. He says it was a poor job. (Advantage if Ludlow asks; disadvantage if the party has already threatened the Company men.)
skillChecks.failure: Doroteo says he's sorry, and goes inside, and shuts the door.

skillChecks.success: The Company men are paid to deny the horses, not to die for them. The two Albuquerque detectives are professionals and will fight only if they must. The four hired guns are cheaper and braver. If the party takes the horses by force, the detectives will draw back and report, and the hired guns will fight.
skillChecks.failure: Six armed men at a gate. It's hard to tell which of them mean it.

skillChecks.success: A mile upstream, the Laguna herd, if Victoriano arranged it. The older herder and his nephew trade six good horses for Ludlow's six blown ones and $60 in silver, in Spanish, without haste and without any interest in the Company. The older man says, as the horses change hands, that Victoriano asked him to tell the party that the cairn at the Cerro Colorado has been put back where it was, by Laguna and by the vecinos of Santa Teresita together, on Friday. He seems to find this satisfying. (Courtesy is the check. Haggling rudely or treating them as anybody's servants ends the trade.)
skillChecks.failure: If there is no arrangement, there is no herd: it's grazing somewhere else this week. If there is one and the party is rude, the herders listen politely and then drive their horses on upstream.

scenes.name: The Flood
scenes.description: Sunday, about four o'clock. Whatever the party has done at the station, they have to cross the Rio Puerco, a quarter-mile of sand with a single wagon ramp on the far bank. The flood comes down at about four: a brown wall of water and trash six feet high, then 1d4 hours of torrent. Cross before it and the Company's men are on the wrong side of a river. Be caught in the bed when it comes, and the coach is swept away unless the team is fresh and the driver is very good. Be caught on the near bank, and the Company's riders come for the chest in the rain, and the party holds the bank with the coach as a fort until the water falls.
scenes.readAloud: The afternoon goes dark at three. Over the mesas to the west the sky has turned the colour of slate, with white veils of rain hanging under it and lightning walking in them, and thunder that you feel in your teeth. The wind comes first, hot and then suddenly cold, smelling of wet earth, and the horses throw up their heads and won't settle. The riverbed is still dry, a quarter-mile of pale sand with a trickle down the middle. Then, from upstream, a sound like a train coming that keeps on getting louder, and the driver on the box looks up the river and says something very short in Spanish. 'Now,' he says. 'Now or not at all.'

skillChecks.success: You hear the flood ten minutes before it arrives, and you know exactly how long a quarter-mile of sand takes at a gallop with six horses and a heavy coach. Long enough, just, if you go now. (Automatic with a Scout's Weather Eye.)
skillChecks.failure: You hear it when everyone hears it, with perhaps three minutes to spare. That's not enough time to cross safely, and maybe enough to cross unsafely.

skillChecks.success: The coach crosses the Puerco ahead of the flood, axle-deep in the trickle and then up the far ramp with the water coming down behind it like a wall. The horses are blowing and the passengers are thrown about, and the Company's riders on the near bank watch you go and can do nothing for two hours. (Disadvantage with a blown team; advantage with Jethro on the box or a fresh Laguna team.)
skillChecks.failure: Halfway across, the flood hits the coach broadside. Everyone makes a STR or DEX save, DC 14, or is swept out; the coach takes 4d10 bludgeoning and drifts. Getting the team, the coach, the chest and the people to the far bank is a scene of ropes, swimmers and horsemanship, and the chest is the first thing the Company's men on the near bank will try to shoot whoever is carrying.

skillChecks.success: Whatever happened in the river, you get the chest, or a witness, or Don Policarpio, out of it alive. Someone goes back for someone. It's the bravest thing anyone does in the campaign, and the coach will tell it at every station for fifty years.
skillChecks.failure: The river takes something: a horse, the evidence box, the prisoner's irons and with them the prisoner. The GM chooses, and it should hurt, and it shouldn't be the act of possession unless the party left it in the riverbed through carelessness.

encounters: The Puerco station: six Company men (two Agency Detectives, four Hired Guns) at the corral, with the roof, the station's adobe walls and the corral for cover. The detectives withdraw if the hired guns are losing

The near bank in the flood: the Company's riders (Road Agent or Hired Gun, about six) come for the chest in the rain, while the party holds the coach and the bank with the river behind them for 1d4 hours

acts.title: Monday 18 July: Ten O'Clock
acts.description: The last eighteen miles and the court. Dawn at the Ceja, and the Company's last throw on the grade down. Atrisco and its farmers. The bridge and the writ. Old Town, the plaza, the bandstand, the courthouse, Montaño with his watch, and the church clock four minutes fast. If Rendell lives, he will be at one of these places. End the campaign in the courtroom, with the judge and the evidence, and let the players hear what each piece is worth.
objectives: Survive the running fight down the Ceja, with the coach and the chest
Get the coach, or at least its passengers and cargo, across the bridge
Reach the courthouse by ten o'clock
Put the evidence, the witnesses and the act of possession before the court, and face Cade Rendell, if he is still standing between you and it

scenes.name: The Ceja
scenes.description: Monday at dawn. The coach changes horses at Casilda Gutiérrez's station at the top of the Ceja: four old sound horses, coffee, and a widow with a shotgun who wants to ride down on the box. Then the long grade down to the valley, and the Company's riders coming over the rim behind on fresh horses: Rendell, if he lives, or Sorrel with six men. It's a chase (combat.json chases), three to five rounds, Animal Handling on the box against their Riding, with complications from the road. The riders want to board the coach and take the chest. Rendell, if he is with them, wants to kill a witness, and if the coach gets away from him he will ride ahead to Old Town and wait.
scenes.readAloud: The coach comes over the lip of the Ceja into the first light, and the whole valley of the Rio Grande opens below you like a map unrolled: green fields and silver acequias, a long dark line of cottonwoods along the river, adobe villages like scattered dice, and, far off across the river, two white church towers and beyond them the smoke of trains. Albuquerque. The road drops away down the face of the escarpment in long loops. A thin grey-haired woman at the little station by the road is holding the heads of four horses and a shotgun, and she says, 'You're late, Don Cyprian. Three years late.' Then somebody on the roof shouts. Over the rim behind you, a mile back and coming fast, are seven riders in a line, and the one in front is riding a tall grey and holding a long rifle across his saddle.

skillChecks.success: The driver takes la Doña down the Ceja as if she were a buggy: the turns on two wheels, the arroyos at a gallop, the freight wagon coming up passed with an inch to spare. Win the chase and the riders fall behind at the foot of the grade, where Atrisco's farmers are coming out with shotguns. (Advantage with Jethro on the box. Each round the riders can shoot at disadvantage, combat.json mounted_combat.)
skillChecks.failure: The riders catch the coach on the lower grade. Two of them try to board from the saddle (Acrobatics DC 15), and one tries for the leaders. It's a fight on a moving coach, and anyone who falls off is in the road with seven horsemen.

skillChecks.success: A rider alongside the coach, Nicanor or Rufina or Venancio or Facundo Ulibarri, turns back into the pursuers on a narrow loop of the grade and holds them for a round, which may be the round that matters. It's brave and very dangerous, and it should be rewarded.
skillChecks.failure: The rider alongside is cut off and has to take another way down. They'll rejoin the coach at the river, or not.

skillChecks.success: In Atrisco you stop, just long enough, and ask for help. A dozen farmers on mules with shotguns and old muskets come out to escort la Doña to the bridge, because they know Ludlow and have heard from a Laguna section hand what the coach is carrying. The Company's riders won't follow you into a village of armed men at seven in the morning.
skillChecks.failure: Atrisco's people watch you go by and cheer, and stay where they are. It's not their fight.

scenes.name: The Bridge
scenes.description: The Rio Grande bridge into Albuquerque, about half past eight. At the toll shed at the far end a deputy constable with a writ of attachment is waiting for the coach and horses of the Rio Seco line, for the Company's $4,000 note, with two Company detectives to help. The writ is lawful. It attaches the coach and horses, not the passengers, the witnesses or the chest. If Darius Crandall's wire came, the deputy has the bank's suspension in his other hand and is very uncomfortable. If not, it is a mile and a half on foot from the bridge to Old Town with the chest, the witnesses, an old man and the prisoners, with an hour and a half to do it. Or the party argues, or pays, or does something else.
scenes.readAloud: The bridge is a long timber trestle on piles over a wide brown river running high with the rains, with a toll shed at the far end and a gate. At the gate, waiting, is a stout young man with a deputy's badge, a paper in his hand and an expression of great unhappiness, and beside him two men in town suits and bowler hats with their coats unbuttoned. As the coach comes off the bridge the deputy steps into the road and holds up the paper. 'Rio Seco Mail and Stage Line? Coach and horses? I have a writ of attachment for them, for a debt of four thousand dollars owed to the Paragon Townsite and Improvement Company. I'm sorry, Mr. Ludlow. I'm truly sorry.' Ludlow climbs down from the step and looks at the paper, and at his coach, and at the church towers across the fields, and doesn't say anything at all.

skillChecks.success: The writ attaches 'the coach, horses, harness and equipment of the said line'. It attaches nothing else. The passengers, the witnesses, the chest and the evidence are not the line's equipment, and the deputy, once it's shown to him, agrees with relief. You can walk. (Book Learning or Montaño's clerk, who is waiting at the bridge, gives advantage.)
skillChecks.failure: The Company's detectives insist that the luggage is the line's equipment. The deputy isn't sure. You'll have to persuade him, or go round him.

skillChecks.success: If Darius Crandall's wire came, the deputy has the bank's suspension of the sale in his other hand and is delighted to have a reason not to do this. He tears up nothing, but he folds the writ, puts it in his pocket and says he'll serve it tomorrow, after he's asked a judge. La Doña goes on into Old Town. If the wire didn't come, the Southwestern Express Company's agent, Milo Thackery, who has ridden out to meet the coach, offers to stand surety for the note against the reward for the box. The deputy takes it.
skillChecks.failure: The deputy serves the writ. La Doña and her horses are attached at the bridge, and the passengers walk.

skillChecks.success: Walking it: a mile and a half through the fields to Old Town with the chest, the evidence, the witnesses, an exhausted old man and the prisoners, in an hour and a half. Carrying the chest between two, the old man between two more, keeping the prisoners in line, you do it with ten minutes to spare. The Company's detectives follow all the way and do nothing, because by now half of Atrisco is walking with you.
skillChecks.failure: You do it, but it takes everything. Every party member who carried something arrives with a level of exhaustion, and you come into the plaza at five to ten by the church clock, which is four minutes fast.

scenes.name: Ten O'Clock
scenes.description: Old Town plaza on a Monday morning. Vendors, carts, lawyers, a band rehearsing on the bandstand, the church towers, the courthouse with its portal and steps, and Licenciado Montaño on the steps with his watch in his hand. If Rendell lives, he's standing by the bandstand with the sun behind the church at his back, alone, waiting to kill a witness on the courthouse steps in front of a city. The party can draw, arrest him (the federal marshals are inside, and a Deputy U.S. Marshal can call them), or be clever. Then the court sits. Judge Maitland takes the grand jury's evidence, Montaño's answer for the grant and the election contests in order, in public, from originals and witnesses. End the campaign in the courtroom, with each piece of evidence read aloud and what it is worth, and then go out onto the plaza into the noon bells.
scenes.readAloud: The plaza is full of morning: a cottonwood, a bandstand, carts of melons and chile and firewood, a priest crossing to the church, a dozen men in frock coats on the courthouse portal with papers under their arms. On the steps a small neat Hispano gentleman in grey, with a white moustache and gold spectacles, holds a watch in his palm and stares at the corner of the plaza as if he could make you appear there by wanting it. Then he sees you, and closes the watch with a snap you can hear across the square, and raises one hand. And between you and him, by the bandstand, in a white shirt with the sun behind the church at his back, a tall fair man straightens up from the rail he has been leaning on, and settles his hat, and smiles. 'Morning,' Cade Rendell says. 'I was beginning to think you'd quit.'

skillChecks.success: The stare-down, on the last morning, in front of a city. Win it, and Rendell has disadvantage on the draw. If a Lawman tells him he's under arrest for the murder of Lon Brisbane and the robbery of the United States mail, and federal marshals come out onto the portal behind you, Rendell has to choose between dying a murderer on the courthouse steps and walking into the courthouse in irons. He looks at the marshals, and at the crowd, and at you, and you will know which before he does.
skillChecks.failure: He has the sun and the crowd and his nerve. It's a showdown (frontier.json showdowns), and he has advantage on the draw unless someone can take the sun out of your eyes.

skillChecks.success: In the courtroom, the evidence goes in in order: the act of possession, read aloud in Spanish and English by Montaño; Tiburcio, steady on the stand; Jethro, who tells it all and asks the court for nothing; the bank's schedule beside a note from a miner's envelope, read by Darius Crandall; Cazenove's bill; Coldiron's letter, read in his own presence. Judge Maitland stays the Company's suit until the Surveyor General reports, takes the election contests under advisement on the poll books, and gives the grand jury what it needs. Coldiron leaves the courtroom before the end. The marshal's men are waiting for him on the portal.
skillChecks.failure: Something the party needed didn't arrive, lost in the river or left at the plaza. The judge does what he can with what he has. Grade the outcome by what reached the court (control file outcomes).

skillChecks.success: When it's over and the court rises for noon, Cyprian Ludlow sits on the courthouse steps in the sun with his hat beside him and his eyes shut. Jethro Petree, in irons, sits beside him, because the marshal let him. Neither says anything. Then the church bells go for noon, and Ludlow says, to nobody, 'Thirteen years and one more run. Never lost a sack.' It isn't true, and everyone on the steps lets him say it.
skillChecks.failure: The court rises. Everyone is very tired. Somewhere a band is playing.

encounters: The Ceja: Cade Rendell (Fast Gun) or Shad Sorrel (Bandit Sharpshooter) with six riders (Hired Gun or Road Agent), a running fight down the grade (combat.json chases and mounted_combat)
Old Town plaza: Cade Rendell (Fast Gun), alone, in front of the courthouse, if he lives. Federal marshals (Federal Marshal) inside the courthouse, if anyone thinks to call them

npcsInvolved.name: Cyprian Ludlow, 66
npcsInvolved.role: Owner of the line; the last run is his
npcsInvolved.description: As before, older this week. He rides inside with a shotgun across his knees, the way he did in 1868.
npcsInvolved.motivation: One more run, his name, and his coach. He'll let the Company take the horses if he must. He won't let them take la Doña while he's alive.

npcsInvolved.name: Jethro Petree, 61
npcsInvolved.role: The inside man, asking to drive
npcsInvolved.description: As before, sober for a week now, thin and grey and very quiet. On the box he is the best driver in the territory, and he knows it is the last time.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To bring her in. Then to tell the court everything and take what comes.

npcsInvolved.name: Rafael Candelaria, 22
npcsInvolved.description: See his sheet. He drives if Jethro doesn't, and rides beside him on the box if Jethro does.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get the coach there, and to forgive the old man, which is the harder of the two.

npcsInvolved.name: Thurman Ames, 52
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, thin, stooped, in a black frock coat, with a lawyer's voice and a leather case. Competent, dry and without illusions about his client.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To win for the Company in court, and to stay well away from anything that happened outside one.

npcsInvolved.name: Doroteo Griego, 63
npcsInvolved.role: Keeper of the Puerco station, now the Company's
npcsInvolved.description: Grey, bent, in a leather apron, with the keys at his belt and his shame on his face. He kept the station for Ludlow for twelve years.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep a roof over his head, and to be able to look at Cyprian Ludlow. He can't do both.

npcsInvolved.name: Bonifacio Ulibarri, 44
npcsInvolved.description: Short, broad, cheerful, in a straw hat, with nine children and the line's last fresh team. Refused the Company's $200.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Don Cyprian's honour and his own. His son Facundo wants to ride with the coach.

npcsInvolved.name: Casilda Gutiérrez, 50
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, grey, upright, a widow who has kept the station for three years for no pay since the contract was cut, with four old horses and a shotgun.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be needed by the line one more time, and to say so.

npcsInvolved.name: Licenciado Ezequiel Montaño, 55
npcsInvolved.description: Small, neat, grey-suited, gold-spectacled, educated in St. Louis, the best land-grant lawyer in the district and the most punctual man in the territory. He has represented eleven grants and won three, which is a good record.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To file the grant's answer with the original act of possession by ten o'clock, and not a minute later.

npcsInvolved.name: Judge Ives Maitland, 60
npcsInvolved.role: Judge of the district court, Albuquerque
npcsInvolved.description: A slow, careful, honest New Englander, white-whiskered, who has sat on the territorial bench for six years and believes in originals, witnesses and order.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To hear everything in its turn and decide on what is put in front of him.

npcsInvolved.name: Darius Crandall, 46
npcsInvolved.role: Cashier, Bank of the Rio Abajo
npcsInvolved.description: A precise, bald, furious little man who was robbed in Kansas in 1874 and has written down every serial number he has handled since. His notes were used to buy votes.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His bank's honour. He'll go to the bridge himself if he has to.

npcsInvolved.name: Milo Thackery, 40
npcsInvolved.description: Brisk, sandy-haired and harassed, with a box to recover and a dead messenger on his conscience.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The box, the robbers, and a reason to tell Lon Brisbane's mother that it meant something.

npcsInvolved.name: Cade Rendell, 38
npcsInvolved.description: As before, alone now, without a paymaster, still vain and still very dangerous.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be the man who stopped the last coach, or failing that, to die famous on the courthouse steps.

npcsInvolved.name: Everard Coldiron, 44
npcsInvolved.role: Manager of the Company, in the courtroom
npcsInvolved.description: As before, in a white suit on the courtroom bench, until his own copybook letter is read aloud.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To leave Albuquerque on the afternoon train before anyone serves him with anything.

rewards.money: The Southwestern Express Company pays its rewards on the grand jury's indictments: $500 for the box's contents recovered (the notes from the envelopes count, and so does whatever coin is found on the gang), and $250 for each robber indicted or killed in the act. Milo Thackery adds $100 'from the messengers of the Southwestern', who took up a collection for Lon. Licenciado Montaño's fee for the grant is paid by the vecinos in sheep, chile and a promise, and he asks the party to accept a share of the chile. Cyprian Ludlow gives la Doña's brass lamps, one each, if he still has her.
items: A brass lamp from coach No. 7, la Doña, if Ludlow still owns her
Judge Maitland's order staying the Company's suit, a certified copy, for the comisión's chest
The grand jury's indictments of Fenton Rusk, Cade Rendell and the gang, and possibly Everard Coldiron
A letter from Laguna Pueblo's governor, through Victoriano Romero, thanking the party in two sentences for witnessing the corner
A lifetime pass, renewed, on the Santa Teresita branch mail route, which does not yet exist and will
Whatever the party chooses to keep of the campaign: a .50 ball, a sombrero, a yellow ticket with no red cross

twists: Jethro Petree on the box is the campaign's best redemption and its biggest risk. If the party lets him drive, he drives as nobody else in the territory can, and he will try to sacrifice himself, on the Ceja or in the river, to save the coach. Let him, if the players don't stop him. If they do stop him, let him live to testify. Either is a good ending for him.

If Fenton Rusk is a prisoner on the coach, Rendell wants him dead more than anyone else on it, because Rusk can hang him and Coldiron both. Rusk knows it. Halfway down the Ceja he begs the party for a gun. Give it to him or not; he is a coward and will use it on whoever is nearest him when he panics.

If the act of possession is lost in the river, the grant's case isn't lost. The 1846 copy in the church chest, Don Policarpio's testimony of seventy years' common use, Rufina's, Don Fermín's if he turned, and Laguna's 1856 boundary agreement naming the corner are enough for Montaño to ask for a stay. It's weaker, and the judge says so. The original was better, and the party should know what it cost.

Coldiron tries to leave on the afternoon train. The marshal's men are on the platform if the copybook letter was read in court. If it wasn't, he goes back to St. Louis, and the Company replaces him with a cleverer man, which the party should feel as a loss.
dmTips: This scenario is a road movie with a courtroom at the end. Run the road as a sequence of set pieces with a clock, the date and the hour always visible, and let the players feel the miles: twenty to La Mesita, twenty more to the Puerco, eighteen to the Ceja, twelve to Old Town.

The choice of who drives matters more than any die roll. If the players let Jethro drive, give him advantage on every Animal Handling check and the whole of the road to earn it back. If they choose Rafael, give Rafael the moment at the flood or on the Ceja when he realises he can do it.

The Company's men want to stop the coach, not to massacre it. A massacre on a public road would bring federal troops. Only Rendell wants to kill, and he wants an audience. Use that: the fights on the road are about horses, the chest and the witnesses, and the killing is saved for the plaza.

The Laguna herd is a trade between equals and should be played as one. The herders are courteous, unhurried, fair and uninterested in the Company's quarrel. The cairn going back on Friday, by both communities together, is news they bring with satisfaction, and it is the only thing they volunteer.

The flood is the river's decision, not the GM's punishment. Tell the players it is coming. Let them hear it and decide. If they cross and make it, it's the campaign's best moment. If they don't, the scene in the water is the second-best.

End in the courtroom, not on the plaza. The showdown with Rendell is the genre's last promise, but the campaign's last word is the evidence being read aloud and what it is worth. Read the act of possession aloud in Spanish. Then let the judge rule.

After the court rises, close with the epilogue line from the control file. In 1897 the Supreme Court will rule against the commons of community grants. What the party won in 1881 may be lost then. Then show the vecinos, still there. Then show la Doña, if Ludlow kept her, carrying the plaza's own mail twice a week on a little branch route, with Rafael on the box and a brass lamp missing from each side.
